blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a longitudinal study by Ren et al. that examines how privacy leaks in Android apps evolve across different versions over an 8-year period. The paper quantifies the concerning trend of worsening privacy practices, with over 50% of apps getting worse in subsequent releases, and only 26.3% improving. Key insights include the shockingly slow adoption of HTTPS (taking up to five years for half of apps to adopt it), the pervasive nature of third-party tracking, and the alarming frequency of PII (Personally Identifiable Information) leaks, including passwords sent in plaintext by some apps. The study tracks various types of PII, such as unique identifiers, locations, and sensitive personal data, revealing that single-version analyses underestimate the total PII collected over an app's lifetime. The authors also demonstrate how rotating PII leaks across versions can build a comprehensive profile of users, raising significant privacy concerns. The paper concludes with recommendations for users to adopt tools like ReCon to block unwanted privacy leaks.
paper_title: Bug fixes, improvements, ... and privacy leaks. A longitudinal study of PII leaks across Android app versions
paper_abstract: Keywords The Android accessibility (a11y) service has been widely utilized by malware to abuse benign services. To prevent such abuse, developers need to secure a11y content access in both their apps and mobile websites. However, a misalignment of a11y protection mechanisms exists between them. Prior research has focused on attacking and defending a11y information embedded in native Android apps. However, our research found that a11y malware can retrieve app-protected a11y information in its mobile browser-rendered website counterpart, leaving mobile browser users more vulnerable to a11y attacks than app users. To help benign service developers vet this attack surface, we developed SOMBRA, an automated analysis pipeline to vet browser-side leakage of a11y information that is a11y-protected in apps. Using SOMBRA, we analyzed 294 benign services and found 29 of them deploy app-side a11y protection mechanisms to secure 256 views. SOMBRA discovered that 241, 402, 244, and 251 elements corresponding to their protected app-side views are a11y-exposed in their websites rendered by Chrome, Firefox, Brave, and Edge browsers, respectively. The leaked elements contain sensitive personal identifiable information. Finally, SOMBRA discovered that most developers do not adopt browser-side a11y protections because existing mechanisms either have ineffective protection or hinder the usability of their content.
